title: The producer's chair
summary: The fourth chair, and the one nobody applauds. They write the motion bank for the family debate they will also judge, decide in one arguable sentence what the four seasons were actually about and plant it in act one, fix the guest list so that every name is either given a job or told there is nothing to prepare, and order the run of show with minutes beside every segment and two answers about the cold open written down.
materials: the Expedition dossier, open at the programme page and the Talk page
the wall map, where the Expedition's date is written
paper and a pencil for the eight motions
the family at the table for the guest list, and a phone for the one question about old recordings

steps.title: The producer's chair
steps.body:
Three chairs so far. You debated, then you judged, then you coached. Today you take the fourth one and it is the one nobody applauds: the producer's chair, where you decide what happens, in what order, and who does it.

A producer is not a performer. Almost nothing a producer does is visible on the day, and if the producing was good the day looks like it organised itself. That is the job. Somebody has to decide what the room is for.

Four jobs this week, and all four are yours to decide rather than yours to guess at.

The motion bank. The family debate at the Grand Expedition runs on a motion, and you write the ones it could be. You will also judge that debate, so you are writing motions you have to be fair about afterwards, which changes what you write.

The through-line. Four seasons is a lot of stuff, and a talk is not stuff. A talk is one thing said with evidence. What were the four seasons actually about? Nobody is allowed to answer that for you. It is your road and it is your sentence.

The guest list, decided with the family, and then the honest thing that comes with it: everybody who is coming is either given a job or told plainly that they have nothing to prepare, because a guest who does not know which of those they are will spend the whole morning quietly worrying.

The run of show. What happens first, what happens next, how many minutes each thing gets, and where the food is.

And this week's question, which is not decoration on the end of the hour. You are about to stand up and talk to a room for ten minutes. That is ten minutes of other people's lives that you asked for. So: what makes something worth saying to a room? Worth saying to a room is not the same as true, and it is not the same as interesting to you. Some true and interesting things are not worth a room's ten minutes, and knowing the difference is most of what a producer is for.

steps.title: The motion bank, and what the four seasons were about
steps.body:
Two pieces of writing, and the second one is the harder one by a long way.

First, the motion bank. Fifteen minutes, in the dossier. Write eight motions. Not three good ones: eight, because the first three are the ones anybody would write and the seventh is usually where the interesting one is hiding.

Four tests, and a motion has to pass all four.

Could a thoughtful person argue either side of it? If one side is obviously right, it is not a motion, it is an announcement.

Is it about one thing? Motions with an and in the middle are two debates wearing one coat, and the round falls apart in the second speech.

Can everybody in the room define every word in it? A motion that turns into an argument about what a word means is a motion nobody enjoyed.

And the coin test, which matters most because you will be judging. If the coin fell the wrong way, would you be content to stand on that bench? If not, you already have a favourite, and a judge with a favourite in the motion is a judge in trouble before anybody has spoken.

Mark the eight. Cross out the ones that failed a test and write which test they failed. Keep the three strongest for the envelope. The envelope gets sealed later; today it is only the bank.

Second, and this is the one to go slowly on. What were the four seasons about?

One sentence. Under ten words if you can manage it. Not a list, not a summary, and not I learned a lot of things, which is true of everybody who has ever been alive. A through-line is a claim. Somebody should be able to hear it and disagree with it, and if nobody could disagree, it is not a through-line, it is weather.

Here is the test to run on your sentence. Take act one, the forest, and ask whether it is evidence for that sentence. Then act three, the mountains. If an act is not evidence, either the act changes or the sentence does, and you decide which.

Then the craft move you have been living inside for three seasons and now get to use on purpose. A talk plants something early and pays it off late. So act one plants your through-line without ever naming it, and act four names it. Write in the dossier which exact line of act one is the plant, because in week 12 nobody, including you, will remember on their own.

Nobody gets to tell you what the sentence is. Not the plan and not the grown-ups. If somebody offers you one, say thank you and write your own.
checklist: Eight motions are written in the dossier, not three
Every rejected motion has the test it failed written next to it, and three survivors are marked
I ran the coin test on all three survivors and I would be content on either bench of each one
The through-line is one sentence, it is a claim somebody could disagree with, and it is mine
The exact line of act one that plants the through-line is written down in the dossier

steps.title: The guest list, and the run of show
steps.body:
Now the producing proper. Dossier open, pencil, and the wall map where you can see the Expedition's date.

The guest list, decided at the table with the family rather than by you alone, because some of these people have to travel and some of them may only be able to join on a call. Write every name down. Then put one of two labels beside each one.

Has a job, and the job written out in a sentence, so they can prepare it.

Nothing to prepare, and somebody tells them so, in those words. A guest who has not been told is a guest who spends the morning quietly wondering whether they are about to be asked something.

Then the rule that keeps the day safe: no segment may need a particular guest in order to happen. People get ill and flights move. If a segment falls apart because one person did not come, redesign the segment now, while it costs you a pencil line.

The run of show. Every segment on its own line, in order, with minutes written beside it, and the minutes added up at the bottom. A programme that does not add up is a programme that finishes in the dark with people looking at their phones.

Four ordering rules worth having.

The thing that needs the most attention goes while the room is freshest, which means early.

The youngest performer goes before people get tired and before the food, not after, and your youngest has a station to run.

Nothing quiet goes straight after eating.

And the thing you want people to leave carrying goes last, because last is what they will still have in the car.

Now the cold open, which is the first thing the room will meet, and it needs two answers this week rather than one.

The first answer is not yours and it is a job for a grown-up: can the oldest recordings actually still be played and copied off whatever they live on? Old files move house badly. Ask this week, not later, because the answer changes what the opening is.

The second answer is entirely yours and nobody may argue with it: do you want a recording of your own younger voice played out loud in front of guests? Yes and no are both complete answers and neither one needs a reason.

Write both answers on the run of show. If the recordings exist and you want them, the talk opens with your own voice from the beginning of all this, played cold to a room that has only ever met the person you are now. If either answer is no, the opening is you reading out, word for word and without improving it, something you actually wrote or said back then, out of the Atlas or the log. It does the same job, because the job is the gap between that person and this one, and reading it aloud shows the gap just as plainly.

Ask your Sprout their own version of the same question, gently, and take their answer as final too. They are being put in front of an audience and nobody has checked whether they want that.
checklist: Every name on the guest list is labelled either with a written job or with nothing to prepare, and somebody is telling that second group so
No segment on the programme needs one particular guest in order to happen
Every segment has minutes beside it and the minutes are added up at the bottom
A grown-up has been asked this week whether the oldest recordings can still be played and copied
My own answer about my old voice, and my Sprout's answer about being watched, are both written on the run of show

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: One take, three parts. First, say your through-line cold, in one sentence, with nothing in front of it and no run-up. Then read your strongest motion out loud and give one honest sentence for each side of it, so anybody listening can hear that it is a real motion and not a lean. Then answer this week's question straight to camera: what makes something worth saying to a room, and what is your reason?
